"The regulator's disclosure requirement effectively prohibited the underlying practice entirely."
"The retailer's margins increased by several percentage points, a gain attributed to better targeting."
"The audit's findings were consistent with, though not conclusive proof of, deliberate discrimination."
"The proxy correlated so strongly with income that regulators dismissed it as completely irrelevant."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "The firm's pricing strategy was granular enough to distinguish between nearly identical customers."**

Granular describes fine-grained detail; being granular enough to separate nearly identical customers is a coherent, natural use of the word. Paragraph (2) praises exactly that rise in the granularity of pricing data. The collocation does not stretch granular beyond fine-grained resolution. Tie the adjective to the passage's point about finer data feeding pricing systems.

Fine-grained discrimination between near-identical customers fits granular, so the wording stands.

**B) "The regulator's disclosure requirement effectively prohibited the underlying practice entirely."**

Disclosure and prohibition are different regulatory moves. Paragraph (7) stresses that the Digital Services Act requires disclosure of personalised prices yet does not prohibit the practice itself; this sentence collapses those two into one. A disclosure mandate often feels as strong as a ban until you separate the verbs. Keep disclose and prohibit apart, as the passage does.

**Trap:** A disclosure mandate often feels as strong as a ban until you separate the verbs.

Requiring disclosure is not prohibiting the practice, so this line fails the ordinary meanings of both words — and the passage's explicit contrast.

**C) "The retailer's margins increased by several percentage points, a gain attributed to better targeting."**

Attributed to is the standard collocation for assigning a reported cause to a result; "several percentage points" also matches how paragraph (3) talks about margin gains. Nothing in the pairing strains English usage. Attributed for or attributed with would be wrong; attributed to is the fixed link. The percentage-points unit also keeps the gain in the same register as the survey.

Attributed to correctly links the margin gain to targeting, so the sentence is sound.

**D) "The audit's findings were consistent with, though not conclusive proof of, deliberate discrimination."**

The hedging frame "consistent with, though not conclusive proof of" is precise academic English: it allows alignment with a hypothesis without upgrading to proof. Paragraph (6) uses the same scaffold for income-based discrimination. Dropping the hedge and saying proved would overstate the audit's claim. Keep both halves of the frame — consistent with, not conclusive proof.

That careful hedge is used correctly, so the wording holds.

**E) "The proxy correlated so strongly with income that regulators dismissed it as completely irrelevant."**

A strong correlation with income would make a proxy more relevant to discrimination concerns, not "completely irrelevant." The so…that result clause reverses the logical force of the correlation claim. So…that can sound fluent while smuggling a nonsensical consequence. Strong income correlation implies relevance; dismissing the proxy as irrelevant fights ordinary meaning.

**Trap:** So…that can sound fluent while smuggling a nonsensical consequence.

Strong income correlation implies relevance, so dismissing the proxy as irrelevant fails ordinary meaning.
highlights: What has changed is the granularity of the data feeding these systems
it does not prohibit the underlying practice itself
personalised pricing increased average retailer margins by approximately 4 to 7 percentage points
consistent with, though not conclusive proof of, income-based discrimination
these proxies can correlate with income, ethnicity, or age

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Short statements testing precise recall of dates, figures, and the theoretical mechanism described, including a calculation-based trap.
statements: Britain fixed the pound at approximately 3.89 pounds per ounce of gold beginning in 1821.
The United States formally committed to a gold standard in law before Germany did.
The price-specie flow mechanism describes automatic self-correction of trade imbalances without deliberate policy intervention.
If global gold production was approximately 5 million ounces in 1890, tripling by 1914 would put 1914 production at approximately 15 million ounces.
The Witwatersrand basin is described as accounting for close to 40% of world gold output by the early 1900s.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Britain fixed the pound at approximately 3.89 pounds per ounce of gold beginning in 1821.**

Paragraph (1) says Britain formally adopted the classical gold standard in 1821 and fixed the pound sterling at approximately 3.89 pounds per fine ounce of gold. The statement copies that date-and-rate pair without changing either figure. Notice that "beginning in 1821" simply restates "formally adopted… in 1821" — it does not invent a later revision of the peg. The passage even adds that the rate remained essentially unchanged for over a century, so nothing in the surrounding sentence undercuts the 1821 / ~3.89 pairing.

**Tip:** Pair the year with the rate in the same sentence — isolated numbers are easier to swap under exam pressure.

The 1821 adoption and ~3.89 rate match paragraph (1) exactly, so the claim is **true**.

**B) The United States formally committed to a gold standard in law before Germany did.**

Paragraph (1) puts Germany on gold convertibility in 1871 after unification and French reparations, while the United States did not formally commit in law until the Gold Standard Act of 1900. That is nearly three decades later, not earlier. The statement's "before Germany" therefore reverses the only two legal-commitment dates the paragraph supplies for those powers. Watch also that "formally… in law" tracks the US wording; Germany's earlier date is still the first of the two named adoptions.

**Trap:** "Before Germany" flips the chronology; the passage's order is Germany first, US last among the named powers.

The statement reverses the 1871 / 1900 sequence, so it is **false** — Germany adopted gold convertibility decades before the US Gold Standard Act.

**C) The price-specie flow mechanism describes automatic self-correction of trade imbalances without deliberate policy intervention.**

Paragraph (2) walks through deficit → gold outflow → tighter money → lower prices → more competitive exports, restoring balance "without any deliberate policy intervention." Economists later named that automatic loop the "price-specie flow mechanism." The statement's "automatic self-correction… without deliberate policy intervention" is therefore a near-paraphrase of both the chain and the label the text assigns to it. Nothing in the paragraph redefines the mechanism as a discretionary policy tool.

The name and the no-intervention self-correction match the passage, so the statement is **true**.

**D) If global gold production was approximately 5 million ounces in 1890, tripling by 1914 would put 1914 production at approximately 15 million ounces.**

Paragraph (3) says global gold production "roughly tripled" between 1890 and 1914. Tripling multiplies by three, so a hypothetical 5 million ounces in 1890 becomes about 15 million in 1914. The arithmetic applies the passage's multiple correctly. The 5 million starting figure is exam scaffolding, not a passage statistic — you only need to multiply that starter by the text's "tripled." Do not confuse the multiple with a percentage-growth gloss such as "grew by 300%."

**Tip:** "Tripled" means ×3 of the starting level, not +3% or +300% of growth language.

The 5 → 15 million application of "roughly tripled" is sound, so the claim is **true**.

**E) The Witwatersrand basin is described as accounting for close to 40% of world gold output by the early 1900s.**

Paragraph (3) credits major discoveries in South Africa's Witwatersrand basin and states that the basin alone was estimated to account for "close to 40% of total world gold output by the early 1900s." The statement restates that share and dating. "Close to 40%" and "early 1900s" are lifted from the same clause, so there is no date swap toward the 1930s exit story later in the passage. The basin's share is also framed as a production fact that eased deflationary pressure, not as a wartime or Depression-era figure.

The ~40% early-1900s Witwatersrand figure is exactly what the passage gives, so the claim is **true**.
highlights: Britain formally adopted the system in 1821, fixing the pound sterling at a rate of approximately 3.89 pounds per fine ounce of gold
did not formally commit to a gold standard in law until the Gold Standard Act of 1900
Economists later termed this selfcorrecting mechanism the "price-specie flow mechanism,"
global gold production roughly tripled between 1890 and 1914
close to 40% of total world gold output by the early 1900s

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Short statements testing wartime financing details, Britain's 1925 return to gold, and a percentage-based math trap.
statements: Britain's wartime spending by 1918 rose to roughly ten times its pre-war annual government expenditure.
Britain returned to gold in 1925 at a rate lower than its pre-war parity.
If Britain's pre-war annual government expenditure was £200 million, ten times that figure would be £1.8 billion.
Keynes argued that Britain's 1925 return to gold at the old rate would force deflation to remain competitive.
The interwar gold exchange standard allowed only gold, not foreign currencies, to serve as reserves.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Britain's wartime spending by 1918 rose to roughly ten times its pre-war annual government expenditure.**

Paragraph (4) says Britain's wartime spending rose to a figure estimated at "roughly ten times its pre-war annual government expenditure by 1918." The multiple and the year line up with the statement. The comparison is to pre-war annual expenditure, not to some other wartime year, so "ten times" stays attached to that baseline. The same paragraph explains why convertibility was abandoned: financing on that scale could not be sustained under strict gold backing.

The ~10× wartime spending claim matches paragraph (4), so it is **true**.

**B) Britain returned to gold in 1925 at a rate lower than its pre-war parity.**

Paragraph (5) is explicit: Britain returned in 1925 "at the pre-war parity of 3.89 pounds per ounce," the same old rate, not a cheaper one. The pain came from restoring that parity while wartime inflation had left British prices ~10% higher relative to America. "Lower than pre-war parity" would mean a devalued peg; the text's critique is the opposite — an overvalued return to 3.89. Churchill's advice from Bank officials is tied to that unchanged parity, not to a reduced one.

**Trap:** "Lower than pre-war parity" invents a devaluation; the passage's point is an overvalued return to the old peg.

Britain restored the identical 3.89 parity, so "lower rate" is **false** — the text says pre-war parity, not a reduced one.

**C) If Britain's pre-war annual government expenditure was £200 million, ten times that figure would be £1.8 billion.**

Paragraph (4) supplies the "roughly ten times" multiple. Ten times £200 million is £2,000 million — £2 billion — not £1.8 billion. The statement misapplies simple multiplication to a plausible-looking answer. The hypothetical £200 million is exam input; the passage only gives the multiple, so the error is pure arithmetic, not a misread year. £1.8 billion would be 9× £200 million, a near-miss distractor built to look "roughly" right.

**Trap:** £1.8 billion is a near-miss distractor; 10 × 200 million is 2,000 million.

The arithmetic is wrong (10 × £200m = £2bn, not £1.8bn), so the claim is **false**.

**D) Keynes argued that Britain's 1925 return to gold at the old rate would force deflation to remain competitive.**

Paragraph (5) records Keynes arguing that restoration at an overvalued rate would "force painful wage and price deflation onto the British economy simply to remain competitive." That is the same critique the statement summarizes. "At the old rate" maps onto the pre-war 3.89 parity the paragraph just named, and "force deflation" tracks Keynes's wage-and-price wording. Historians later treating the prediction as substantially vindicated does not change what Keynes argued at the time.

Keynes's deflation prediction matches the passage, so the statement is **true**.

**E) The interwar gold exchange standard allowed only gold, not foreign currencies, to serve as reserves.**

Paragraph (6) says the interwar arrangement let countries hold "not only gold itself but also foreign currencies, chiefly pounds sterling and US dollars," as reserve backing. "Only gold" is the opposite of that layered design. The classical contrast in the same paragraph — Britain alone holding gold at the core — is what people wrongly paste onto the 1920s rules. The layering of sterling and dollar promises is exactly the vulnerability the text highlights next.

**Trap:** Classical-system gold-only habits get wrongly pasted onto the interwar "gold exchange" rules.

The passage allows sterling and dollars as reserves alongside gold, so "only gold" is **false**.
highlights: Britain's wartime spending, for instance, rose to a figure estimated at roughly ten times its pre-war annual government expenditure by 1918
Britain famously returned to the gold standard in 1925 at the pre-war parity of 3.89 pounds per ounce
roughly ten times its pre-war annual government expenditure by 1918
this restoration at an overvalued rate would force painful wage and price deflation onto the British economy simply to remain competitive
hold not only gold itself but also foreign currencies, chiefly pounds sterling and US dollars

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Short statements testing the 1930s collapse details, including a percentage-calculation trap regarding the dollar's devaluation.
statements: The pound fell by approximately 25% against gold-backed currencies after Britain left gold in 1931.
The dollar was devalued from $20.67 to $35.00 per ounce, an adjustment of roughly 69%.
If the devaluation had instead been exactly 50%, the new gold price from $20.67 would be approximately $31.00.
France was the first major country to abandon gold convertibility in the 1930s.
Historians are described as being in full agreement that the war alone caused the gold standard's collapse.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The pound fell by approximately 25% against gold-backed currencies after Britain left gold in 1931.**

Paragraph (7) says that after Britain abandoned gold in September 1931, "the pound's value fell by approximately 25% against gold-backed currencies within a matter of months." The percentage and the aftermath timing match. The comparison basket is gold-backed currencies, not an undefined "all currencies," and the fall is measured in months, not a single session. "After Britain left gold in 1931" correctly follows the September permanent exit named in the same sentence.

The ~25% post-exit decline is stated outright, so the claim is **true**.

**B) The dollar was devalued from $20.67 to $35.00 per ounce, an adjustment of roughly 69%.**

Paragraph (7) gives both endpoints — $20.67 to $35.00 under the Gold Reserve Act of 1934 — and calls the move "an adjustment of roughly 69%." Checking the math: (35 − 20.67) / 20.67 ≈ 69.3%, which agrees with the text's approximate figure. The statement does not invent a third price; it only repeats the two figures and the passage's own percentage gloss. Roosevelt's stated aim — raising domestic prices against Depression deflation — sits beside those numbers but does not change them.

The stated prices and ~69% adjustment match the passage, so the statement is **true**.

**C) If the devaluation had instead been exactly 50%, the new gold price from $20.67 would be approximately $31.00.**

Using the passage's old price of $20.67, a hypothetical 50% rise is 20.67 × 1.5 ≈ 31.005, which rounds to about $31.00. The item only asks whether that alternative arithmetic is correct, not whether 50% was the real 1934 change. Keep $20.67 as the base from the Gold Reserve Act sentence; multiply by 1.5 only for the "what if" branch. The historical ~69% move to $35.00 is a separate fact and must not overwrite this counterfactual.

**Tip:** Separate the passage's actual ~69% move from the exam's "what if 50%" calculation.

The 50% hypothetical from $20.67 correctly lands near $31, so the claim is **true**.

**D) France was the first major country to abandon gold convertibility in the 1930s.**

Paragraph (8) calls France "the last major holdout," abandoning gold convertibility in 1936. Britain had already left permanently in 1931, and the US suspended domestic convertibility in 1933 — both before France. "First" therefore swaps France's landmark end-date for the wrong rank in the exit sequence. The same sentence yokes France's 1936 exit to the classical era being "in every meaningful sense, over," which only makes sense if others had already gone.

**Trap:** "First" swaps France's landmark end-date for the wrong rank in the exit sequence.

France was the last major holdout in 1936, not the first, so the statement is **false**.

**E) Historians are described as being in full agreement that the war alone caused the gold standard's collapse.**

Paragraph (8) says historians "remain divided" over whether collapse mainly followed World War I's disruption of fundamentals or showed that gold, without pre-1914 cooperative props, could not self-correct under a major shock. "Full agreement" and "the war alone" both overstate what the text allows. One camp emphasizes wartime disruption; the other questions whether the standard could self-correct once informal cooperation was gone — neither reading is presented as unanimous. The earlier golden-age discussion of Bank of England coordination is the "cooperative arrangements" side of that debate.

The passage stresses division, not consensus, so the claim is **false** — historians remain divided, not united behind a war-only story.
highlights: the pound's value fell by approximately 25% against gold-backed currencies within a matter of months
devalued the dollar from $20.67 to $35.00 per ounce of gold, an adjustment of roughly 69%
devalued the dollar from $20.67 to $35.00 per ounce of gold
when France, the last major holdout, also abandoned gold convertibility
Historians remain divided as to whether the system's collapse should be understood

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Short statements testing whether percentage changes and the sequence of events across decades have been subtly altered.
statements: Global gold production roughly tripled between 1890 and 1914, meaning it grew by approximately 300%.
The Gold Standard Act, formally committing the US to gold in law, was passed before Germany adopted gold convertibility in 1871.
If Britain's prices were 10% higher than America's relative to the old fixed rate, a good priced at $100 in America would need to sell at $90 in Britain to match that gap.
Britain abandoned the gold standard permanently in 1931, several years after the US suspended domestic gold convertibility in 1933.
The Bank of England's discount rate served as a coordinating signal that other central banks frequently followed during the system's golden age.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Global gold production roughly tripled between 1890 and 1914, meaning it grew by approximately 300%.**

Paragraph (3) does say production "roughly tripled," but tripling means the new level is 300% of the old level — an increase of 200%, not growth "by approximately 300%." The statement confuses a multiple with a percentage-increase label. If output goes from 100 to 300, you have tripled (×3) and grown by 200%, not by 300%. The Witwatersrand share sentence nearby does not redefine "tripled," so the error is purely in the "meaning it grew by…" gloss.

**Trap:** "Tripled" ≠ "+300% growth"; a 100 → 300 move is +200%.

The multiple is right but the +300% gloss is wrong, so the claim is **false**.

**B) The Gold Standard Act, formally committing the US to gold in law, was passed before Germany adopted gold convertibility in 1871.**

Paragraph (1) dates German convertibility to 1871 and the US Gold Standard Act to 1900. The US law came decades after Germany's adoption, not before it. "Formally committing… in law" correctly echoes the Act's wording, but "before Germany… in 1871" still reverses the sequence. Earlier US "bimetallic experiments" mentioned in the same paragraph are not the 1900 legal gold commitment, so they cannot rescue a "before 1871" claim.

The chronology is reversed (1871 Germany, 1900 US Act), so the statement is **false**.

**C) If Britain's prices were 10% higher than America's relative to the old fixed rate, a good priced at $100 in America would need to sell at $90 in Britain to match that gap.**

Paragraph (5) says wartime inflation left British prices "roughly 10% higher, relative to America's," than the old fixed rate could support. A 10% higher British price level maps a $100 US good to about $110 in Britain, not $90. The statement flips the direction of the gap. Higher UK prices are why restoring the old 3.89 parity looked overvalued and invited deflation — a $90 UK sticker would understate, not match, that premium.

**Trap:** Higher British prices mean a higher UK sticker, not a $90 discount.

The 10% premium points to ~$110, not $90, so the claim is **false**.

**D) Britain abandoned the gold standard permanently in 1931, several years after the US suspended domestic gold convertibility in 1933.**

Paragraph (7) places Britain's permanent exit in September 1931 and the US suspension in 1933 — Britain left first, then the United States "held on longer." "Several years after" reverses that order. The years themselves (1931 / 1933) are correct; only the relational word "after" is wrong. Roosevelt's 1934 Gold Reserve Act devaluation comes even later and cannot push Britain's exit behind 1933.

**Trap:** The true years (1931 / 1933) are kept, but "after" wrongly stacks Britain behind the US.

Britain left in 1931, two years before the US move in 1933, so "after" makes the statement **false**.

**E) The Bank of England's discount rate served as a coordinating signal that other central banks frequently followed during the system's golden age.**

Paragraph (3) says that in the ~1870–1914 golden age, London was the financial center and "the Bank of England's discount rate served as a coordinating signal that other central banks frequently followed." The statement restates that coordination role. This is exactly the "beyond the automatic mechanism" cooperation the paragraph stresses, and paragraph (8) later calls such informal arrangements what had quietly sustained the system before 1914. The claim does not invent a formal treaty — only the discount-rate followership the text names.

The discount-rate signal is exactly what paragraph (3) describes, so the claim is **true**.
highlights: global gold production roughly tripled between 1890 and 1914
did not formally commit to a gold standard in law until the Gold Standard Act of 1900
British prices roughly 10% higher, relative to America's
in 1931, Britain abandoned the gold standard permanently in September of that year
the Bank of England's discount rate served as a coordinating signal that other central banks frequently followed

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Short statements combining specific rates, dates, and calculated magnitudes, each engineered to sound correct at a glance.
statements: The pound's decline of approximately 25% against gold-backed currencies occurred within months of Britain's September 1931 departure from gold.
If the pound had instead fallen by exactly one third against gold-backed currencies, this would represent a larger decline than the 25% actually recorded.
The Witwatersrand basin's roughly 40% share of world gold output was reached by the early 1930s, shortly before Britain left gold.
France abandoned gold convertibility in 1936, the same year the classical gold standard era is described as having definitively ended.
The dollar's devaluation under the Gold Reserve Act represented a rise in the gold price of exactly $14.33 per ounce.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The pound's decline of approximately 25% against gold-backed currencies occurred within months of Britain's September 1931 departure from gold.**

Paragraph (7) ties the September 1931 permanent exit to a fall of "approximately 25% against gold-backed currencies within a matter of months." Timing, size, and comparison basket all match the statement. "Within months" paraphrases "within a matter of months" without shrinking the window to hours or a single session. The Central European banking crises that precede Britain's exit in the same paragraph supply context but do not change the 25% figure.

The ~25% decline within months of the September exit is what the passage reports, so the claim is **true**.

**B) If the pound had instead fallen by exactly one third against gold-backed currencies, this would represent a larger decline than the 25% actually recorded.**

One third is about 33.3%, which is larger than the passage's recorded ~25%. The item only compares a hypothetical one-third drop with the actual approximate figure; it does not rewrite the historical percentage. Treat ~25% as the fixed baseline from paragraph (7), then ask only whether ⅓ exceeds that baseline. No other passage percentage (for example the dollar's ~69% move) belongs in this comparison.

**Tip:** Keep the passage's 25% as the baseline; then ask whether ⅓ > 25%.

A one-third fall is numerically larger than 25%, so the comparison is **true**.

**C) The Witwatersrand basin's roughly 40% share of world gold output was reached by the early 1930s, shortly before Britain left gold.**

Paragraph (3) dates the Witwatersrand's "close to 40%" share to "the early 1900s," not the early 1930s. Sliding the statistic forward three decades toward Britain's 1931 exit invents a false chronological link. The production surge belongs with the 1890–1914 golden-age discussion, not with the Depression-era exits in paragraph (7). "Shortly before Britain left gold" is extra glue that the passage never attaches to the Witwatersrand figure.

**Trap:** Early 1900s ≠ early 1930s; the later decade appears elsewhere and invites the swap.

The ~40% share is early 1900s in the text, so "early 1930s" makes the claim **false**.

**D) France abandoned gold convertibility in 1936, the same year the classical gold standard era is described as having definitively ended.**

Paragraph (8) opens: "By 1936, when France, the last major holdout, also abandoned gold convertibility, the classical gold standard era was, in every meaningful sense, over." France's 1936 exit and the era's end are the same narrative beat. "Last major holdout" confirms that earlier exits (Britain 1931, US 1933) had already happened, so 1936 is the closing date, not a first exit. The historians' debate that follows concerns causes of collapse, not whether 1936 marks the end.

The passage yokes 1936 France with the definitive end of the classical era, so the statement is **true**.

**E) The dollar's devaluation under the Gold Reserve Act represented a rise in the gold price of exactly $14.33 per ounce.**

Paragraph (7) moves the dollar gold price from $20.67 to $35.00. Subtract: 35.00 − 20.67 = 14.33. The statement's "exactly $14.33" is the correct arithmetic difference between those stated prices. This absolute rise is consistent with the passage's "roughly 69%" relative adjustment; both describe the same $20.67 → $35.00 step. The item does not ask for a new endpoint — only for the gap between the two given figures.

$35.00 − $20.67 = $14.33, so the magnitude claim is **true**.
highlights: abandoned the gold standard permanently in September of that year, and the pound's value fell by approximately 25%
approximately 25% against gold-backed currencies
close to 40% of total world gold output by the early 1900s
By 1936, when France, the last major holdout, also abandoned gold convertibility
devalued the dollar from $20.67 to $35.00 per ounce of gold

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Gold Standard Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the gold standard passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had Britain not returned to gold at the pre-war parity, Keynes's predicted deflation might have been avoided."
"The committee insisted that convertibility is restored before the end of the year."
"The number of countries abandoning gold convertibility continue to rise throughout the 1930s."
"Neither the Bank of England nor other central banks were fully able to prevent the crisis."
"Having suspended convertibility, the currency's value was immediately devalued by the government."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had Britain not returned to gold at the pre-war parity, Keynes's predicted deflation might have been avoided."**

This is a well-formed third conditional with subject–auxiliary inversion: Had + subject + past participle in the if-clause, and a modal perfect ("might have been avoided") in the result clause. No auxiliary is missing, and the participle/modal pairing fits a counterfactual past. The inverted Had-clause stands in for "If Britain had not returned…," which is the standard exam pattern for past counterfactuals. Vocabulary such as pre-war parity and deflation is topical but does not change the grammar verdict.

Inverted Had + past participle with modal perfect is the standard third-conditional pattern, so the sentence is **true**.

**B) "The committee insisted that convertibility is restored before the end of the year."**

After insist + that, formal exam English wants the mandative subjunctive — base form "be," not indicative "is." Repair to "The committee insisted that convertibility be restored before the end of the year." Verbs of demand or recommendation (insist, demand, recommend) commonly trigger this bare-stem pattern in that-clauses. "Is restored" looks like ordinary present tense and is the classic distractor after such verbs.

**Trap:** "Is restored" looks like an ordinary present after that-clause verbs that actually demand the bare subjunctive.

Insist that requires the base subjunctive, so the line is **false** — "…that convertibility be restored…."

**C) "The number of countries abandoning gold convertibility continue to rise throughout the 1930s."**

"The number of" is a singular subject, so the verb must be singular: "continues," not "continue." Repair to "The number of countries abandoning gold convertibility continues to rise throughout the 1930s." Contrast "a number of countries continue…," where the plural noun heads the subject; here the head is number. The -ing phrase "abandoning gold convertibility" modifies countries and does not control agreement.

**Trap:** The nearby plural "countries" tempts agreement with the wrong noun.

Subject–verb agreement fails with "the number… continue," so this is **false** — use "continues."

**D) "Neither the Bank of England nor other central banks were fully able to prevent the crisis."**

With neither…nor, the verb agrees with the nearer subject. Here "other central banks" is plural, so "were" is the right choice. The correlative structure is clean and the agreement rule is applied correctly. Had the nearer noun been singular ("nor the Bank of France"), the verb would shift to was — proximity, not the first noun, decides. Gold-standard vocabulary does not alter the neither…nor rule.

Nearest-subject agreement with plural "central banks" justifies "were," so the sentence is **true**.

**E) "Having suspended convertibility, the currency's value was immediately devalued by the government."**

The opening participle "Having suspended convertibility" must modify the subject that did the suspending. As written, the subject is "the currency's value," which cannot suspend convertibility — a classic dangling modifier. Repair by making the government the subject: "Having suspended convertibility, the government immediately devalued the currency." Passive "was… devalued" hides the agent and makes the dangling more likely; restoring an active institutional subject fixes both clarity and grammar.

**Trap:** A passive main clause after an active participle often leaves the agent orphaned.

The dangling participle attaches the wrong actor, so the line is **false** — restore a human/institutional subject for the -ing phrase.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the pound fallen than confidence in sterling began to weaken further."
"The Bank of England, along with several allied institutions, were coordinating discount rates."
"Each of the major powers have committed to a fixed gold rate by 1900."
"By the time France abandoned gold in 1936, the classical system will have already collapsed."
"The reserves, which were held partly in foreign currencies, exposed the system to cascading crises."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the pound fallen than confidence in sterling began to weaken further."**

"No sooner…than" correctly triggers inversion: auxiliary Had + subject + past participle, then than + a simple-past follow-on. The sequence (fall, then further weakening) sits in the expected past-perfect → past-simple frame. Do not replace than with when — "no sooner…when" is a common exam error. The inverted Had after no sooner is required; "No sooner the pound had fallen" without inversion would be wrong.

No sooner + inversion + than is formed correctly here, so the sentence is **true**.

**B) "The Bank of England, along with several allied institutions, were coordinating discount rates."**

"Along with several allied institutions" is a parenthetical add-on; the grammatical subject remains singular "The Bank of England," so the verb should be "was coordinating," not "were." Repair: "The Bank of England, along with several allied institutions, was coordinating discount rates." Phrases with along with, as well as, or together with never make a plural subject by themselves. Only a true compound ("The Bank of England and several allied institutions") would license were.

**Trap:** Material after along with/as well as does not make a plural subject.

Singular Bank of England needs "was," so "were" makes the line **false**.

**C) "Each of the major powers have committed to a fixed gold rate by 1900."**

"Each of" takes a singular verb even when a plural noun follows. Prefer "has committed," not "have." Repair: "Each of the major powers has committed to a fixed gold rate by 1900." Every, each, and either similarly pull singular agreement despite a plural of-phrase. The "by 1900" time stamp is topical color; it does not change the each-of rule.

**Trap:** "Powers" looks plural, but each of still governs singular agreement.

Each of + have breaks singular agreement, so the sentence is **false** — "has committed."

**D) "By the time France abandoned gold in 1936, the classical system will have already collapsed."**

"By the time France abandoned…" anchors a past viewpoint, so the main clause needs past perfect ("had already collapsed"), not future perfect ("will have already collapsed"). Future perfect belongs with a still-ahead deadline, not a finished 1936 narrative. Match the tense of the by-the-time clause: past abandoned → past perfect had collapsed. Will have would fit only something like "By the time France abandons…" with a future frame.

**Trap:** "By the time" can tempt will have even when the time clause is already past.

A past by-the-time frame rejects will have, so this is **false** — "…the classical system had already collapsed."

**E) "The reserves, which were held partly in foreign currencies, exposed the system to cascading crises."**

The non-restrictive which-clause correctly modifies plural "reserves," and "were held" agrees with that plural noun. The main verb "exposed" also matches the plural subject. Relative-clause agreement and punctuation are in order. Commas around which mark non-restrictive extra information; that pattern fits a descriptive aside about how reserves were held. The interwar gold-exchange idea of foreign-currency reserves is vocabulary only — the grammar verdict rests on plural agreement.

Plural reserves + "which were held" agree cleanly, so the sentence is **true**.

tasks.title: Task 8
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Historians remain divided as to whether the collapse resulted primarily from wartime disruption."
"Despite of the theoretical self-correcting mechanism, the system depended on informal cooperation."
"Whoever restores convertibility at an overvalued rate risks forcing painful deflation on the economy."
"Churchill denied having fully considered the deflationary consequences of the decision."
"There is several factors that explain the system's stability before 1914."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Historians remain divided as to whether the collapse resulted primarily from wartime disruption."**

"Remain divided as to whether…" correctly introduces an embedded yes/no question after as to. Tense and subject–verb agreement are fine, and whether (not if) is a natural choice after a prepositional as to. The structure mirrors paragraph (8)'s "remain divided as to whether," so the grammar matches the passage's own phrasing pattern. No subjunctive or inversion is required in this embedded whether-clause.

The as to whether structure is well formed, so the sentence is **true**.

**B) "Despite of the theoretical self-correcting mechanism, the system depended on informal cooperation."**

Despite never takes of; that of belongs with in spite of. Repair to "Despite the theoretical self-correcting mechanism…" or "In spite of the theoretical self-correcting mechanism…." Despite behaves like a preposition taking a noun phrase directly; adding of doubles the preposition incorrectly. The content about self-correction versus cooperation echoes the passage, but the preposition error alone makes the line ungrammatical.

**Trap:** Despite / in spite of get blended into the ungrammatical "despite of."

"Despite of" is not standard English, so the line is **false** — drop of or switch to in spite of.

**C) "Whoever restores convertibility at an overvalued rate risks forcing painful deflation on the economy."**

Whoever correctly heads a subject noun clause, and the main verb "risks" agrees with that singular -ever subject. "Risks forcing" (risk + -ing) is the expected pattern after risk. Do not write "risk to force"; risk takes a gerund, not a to-infinitive, in this sense. Whoever (like everyone who) is treated as singular even though it refers to an indefinite person.

Whoever + singular risks + -ing is grammatical, so the sentence is **true**.

**D) "Churchill denied having fully considered the deflationary consequences of the decision."**

After deny, a perfect gerund ("having fully considered") correctly marks an earlier completed action the speaker rejects. Word order and aspect are appropriate for denying a prior consideration. Deny + -ing (or deny + that-clause) is standard; a bare infinitive after deny would be wrong here. The perfect gerund having considered places the alleged consideration before the denying, which fits the meaning.

Denied + perfect gerund is the right pattern here, so the wording is **true**.

**E) "There is several factors that explain the system's stability before 1914."**

Existential there must agree with the notional subject that follows. "Several factors" is plural, so the verb must be "are," not "is." Repair: "There are several factors that explain the system's stability before 1914." There is / there are is decided by the noun after the verb, not by a default singular habit. The relative clause "that explain…" correctly takes a plural verb matching factors once the existential is fixed.

**Trap:** There is feels default until the plural noun after it is noticed.

Plural factors need There are, so "There is several" is **false**.

tasks.title: Task 9
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage's actual vocabulary. Decide if the word/phrase is used correctly according to its meaning as established in the text.
statements: "The mechanism was described as self-correcting, requiring constant deliberate government intervention to function."
"Analysts describe Britain's 1925 return to gold as vindicated by subsequent economic difficulties."
"The gold discoveries eased what might otherwise have been a persistently deflationary bias in the system."
"The interwar arrangement was considerably more fragile than its prewar predecessor, collapsing rapidly under stress."
"The pound's decline was confined to a single trading session, lasting only a few hours in total."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "The mechanism was described as self-correcting, requiring constant deliberate government intervention to function."**

In paragraph (2), the self-correcting price-specie flow restores balance "without any deliberate policy intervention." Pairing "self-correcting" with "constant deliberate government intervention" contradicts the passage sense of the term. The automatic deficit → gold outflow → price → export loop is precisely what makes intervention unnecessary in the model. Any paraphrase that reintroduces constant government action is an antonym of the text's collocation.

**Trap:** Self-correcting sounds technical enough to hide an antonym paraphrase.

Self-correcting means no deliberate intervention, so the sentence's meaning is **false** against the text.

**B) "Analysts describe Britain's 1925 return to gold as vindicated by subsequent economic difficulties."**

Paragraph (5) says many historians regard Keynes's prediction as "substantially vindicated" by Britain's subdued growth and elevated unemployment after the overvalued 1925 return. Here "vindicated" keeps that confirmed-by-later-outcomes sense tied to those difficulties. The verb does not mean the policy was wise; it means later evidence supported the critical forecast. Subdued growth and elevated unemployment in the remainder of the 1920s are the passage's own confirming outcomes.

**Tip:** Vindicated = later evidence bore the claim out — not "justified as wise policy."

The passage-backed use of vindicated fits, so the wording is **true**.

**C) "The gold discoveries eased what might otherwise have been a persistently deflationary bias in the system."**

Paragraph (3) says the Witwatersrand-driven production surge was "easing what might otherwise have been a persistently deflationary bias in a system reliant on a fixed physical commodity." The sentence restates that easing role with the same collocates. "Eased" / "persistently deflationary bias" are the passage's own pairing, not a new causal claim. The discoveries matter because a fixed gold stock would otherwise have kept money tight as economies grew.

The eased / persistently deflationary bias wording matches the passage, so the claim is **true**.

**D) "The interwar arrangement was considerably more fragile than its prewar predecessor, collapsing rapidly under stress."**

Paragraph (6) opens by saying the interwar gold exchange standard "proved considerably more fragile than its prewar predecessor," and later paragraphs show that fragility under 1930s stress. "Considerably more fragile" is the passage's own comparison. Multi-currency reserve layering — sterling and dollars alongside gold — is the structural reason the text gives for that extra fragility. "Collapsing rapidly under stress" summarizes the early-1930s cascade without inventing a new date.

The fragility contrast is passage-true, so the statement is **true**.

**E) "The pound's decline was confined to a single trading session, lasting only a few hours in total."**

Paragraph (7) places the ~25% fall "within a matter of months," not inside one session of a few hours. The sentence invents an ultra-short collapse the text never describes. Months is the only duration the passage attaches to that decline; hours or a single session have no support. Do not borrow "dramatic fashion" from the same paragraph as a license to shrink the timeline.

**Trap:** Months → hours shrinks the timeline without any supporting span.

The passage times the decline in months, so the few-hours version is **false**.
highlights: restoring balance without any deliberate policy intervention
a prediction many economic historians now regard as substantially vindicated by Britain's subdued growth and elevated unemployment
easing what might otherwise have been a persistently deflationary bias
The interwar gold exchange standard proved considerably more fragile than its prewar predecessor
the pound's value fell by approximately 25% against gold-backed currencies within a matter of months

tasks.title: Task 10
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly written, using a word or phrase echoing the passage. Decide if the word/ phrase is used correctly according to its meaning as established in the text.
statements: "The devaluation was an explicit effort to raise domestic price levels and combat deflationary pressures."
"The system's golden age depended heavily on cooperative arrangements beyond the automatic mechanism alone."
"A cascading crisis of convertibility means that confidence problems remained isolated to a single country."
"The layering of reserve promises across multiple currencies increased, rather than reduced, systemic vulnerability."
"Britain's wartime spending is described as having stayed roughly level with pre-war annual expenditure."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "The devaluation was an explicit effort to raise domestic price levels and combat deflationary pressures."**

Paragraph (7) describes Roosevelt's gold move as made "in an explicit effort to raise domestic price levels and combat the deflationary pressures of the Great Depression." The sentence's purpose language tracks that phrasing. "Explicit effort" plus raise prices / fight deflation is the Act's stated policy aim, not a later historian's gloss. The $20.67 → $35.00 numbers sit in the same sentence but are not required to judge this purpose paraphrase.

The raise-prices / fight-deflation purpose matches the passage, so the wording is **true**.

**B) "The system's golden age depended heavily on cooperative arrangements beyond the automatic mechanism alone."**

Paragraph (3) stresses that golden-age stability "depended heavily on factors beyond the automatic mechanism itself," including London's role and cooperative following of the Bank of England's discount rate. Paragraph (8) later names the "informal cooperative arrangements" that had sustained the system before 1914. The statement's "cooperative arrangements beyond the automatic mechanism" therefore stitches those two passage ideas without adding new institutions. Price-specie flow alone is not presented as a sufficient explanation of 1870–1914 stability.

Cooperation beyond the automatic model is exactly the passage's caveat, so the claim is **true**.

**C) "A cascading crisis of convertibility means that confidence problems remained isolated to a single country."**

Paragraph (6) says a loss of confidence in sterling or the dollar could "trigger a cascading crisis of convertibility across many countries simultaneously." Cascading means spread, not isolation — the sentence invents the opposite definition. "Across many countries simultaneously" is the key collocates that block any single-country reading. The classical system's lesser vulnerability is contrasted precisely because it lacked that multi-country layering.

**Trap:** Cascading sounds dramatic but always implies multi-link spillover, not containment.

Cascading crisis = multi-country spillover, so "isolated to a single country" is **false**.

**D) "The layering of reserve promises across multiple currencies increased, rather than reduced, systemic vulnerability."**

Paragraph (6) explains that holding gold plus foreign currencies as reserves meant confidence loss could cascade across many countries — "a vulnerability the classical system had not shared to nearly the same degree." Layering promises raised exposure; it did not dampen it. Sterling and dollar reserves as backing are the "multiple currencies" the statement names. The classical contrast — gold concentrated at Britain's core — underscores that the interwar design added risk.

The passage treats multi-currency layering as more vulnerable, so the statement is **true**.

**E) "Britain's wartime spending is described as having stayed roughly level with pre-war annual expenditure."**

Paragraph (4) says wartime spending rose to "roughly ten times" pre-war annual government expenditure by 1918. "Roughly level" erases that massive multiple. "Roughly" in the passage softens the estimate of a tenfold jump; it does not mean spending stayed flat. That scale of financing is why belligerents abandoned convertibility rather than funding war under strict gold rules.

**Trap:** Roughly softens the scale but cannot flip tenfold growth into flat spending.

The text says ~10×, not level, so the claim is **false**.
highlights: in an explicit effort to raise domestic price levels and combat the deflationary pressures of the Great Depression
depended heavily on factors beyond the automatic mechanism itself
trigger a cascading crisis of convertibility across many countries simultaneously
This layering of promises meant that a loss of confidence in sterling or the dollar could, in principle, trigger a cascading crisis
rose to a figure estimated at roughly ten times its pre-war annual government expenditure by 1918

tasks.title: Task 1
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The just-in-time inventory model is described as having been newly invented in response to the pandemic's disruptions.
The pandemic is described as having exposed, rather than created, a vulnerability that had already been building for decades.
The 2023 survey found that 62% of executives reported reshoring/nearshoring activity, up from a 24% baseline reported in a comparable 2019 survey.
Mexico's appeal as a nearshoring destination is attributed in the passage to matching US wage levels rather than to geographic proximity and cost savings.
The passage attributes the entire FDI increase into Mexico solely to reduced exposure to transpacific shipping disruptions, excluding any other named cause.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The just-in-time inventory model is described as having been newly invented in response to the pandemic's disruptions.**

Paragraph 1 places just-in-time models in the past tense of long-standing practice: firms "had organised" supply chains around single-source suppliers using those models "for decades." The pandemic is the shock that made the existing model fail, not the moment inventing it. The wording "had been building quietly for decades" locks the vulnerability — and the inventory practice behind it — into the pre-2020 timeline.

**Trap:** A crisis that reveals a practice can feel like it created the practice — chronology here runs the other way. Watch for "newly" or "in response to" when the text only says a shock exposed what was already in place.

The claim invents a post-pandemic origin the text never gives, so it fails against the decades-old framing.

**B) The pandemic is described as having exposed, rather than created, a vulnerability that had already been building for decades.**

The opening sentence of Paragraph 1 says the pandemic "exposed a structural vulnerability that had been building quietly for decades." "Exposed" is the key verb: the weakness pre-existed; COVID made it visible. "Rather than created" in the claim simply restates that contrast — the passage never says the pandemic invented the vulnerability.

That wording matches the claim exactly, so the statement tracks the passage. Anchor on the verb "exposed" plus the decades clause whenever the item asks created versus revealed.

**C) The 2023 survey found that 62% of executives reported reshoring/nearshoring activity, up from a 24% baseline reported in a comparable 2019 survey.**

Paragraph 2 pairs the figures and years without mixing them: 62% in the 2023 survey versus 24% in a comparable 2019 survey, for reshoring or nearshoring at least part of production. The phrase "a sharp rise from just 24%" is the passage's own up-from framing, so the claim's "up from" paraphrase stays faithful.

**Tip:** Keep the year stuck to its percentage — swapping 62% onto 2019 is a common trap. Also keep "comparable survey" — the text does not invent a second, unrelated poll.

Both percentages and both years line up with the text, so the claim holds.

**D) Mexico's appeal as a nearshoring destination is attributed in the passage to matching US wage levels rather than to geographic proximity and cost savings.**

Paragraph 3 credits Mexico with "geographic proximity without the full cost of domestic production," and ties FDI growth to lower transport costs and less transpacific disruption exposure. Wage parity with the US is never offered as the reason. The passage's "without the full cost" language is about staying cheaper than US domestic production, not about Mexican wages catching up to US wages.

The statement swaps in an invented wage-match motive, so it fails. If an item substitutes wage convergence for proximity and transport savings, reject it.

**E) The passage attributes the entire FDI increase into Mexico solely to reduced exposure to transpacific shipping disruptions, excluding any other named cause.**

Paragraph 3 says the rise was "driven partly by lower transportation costs and reduced exposure to transpacific shipping disruptions." Two causes are named, and "partly" already blocks an exclusive single-cause reading. "Lower transportation costs" sits beside the shipping-disruption clause, so dropping that first driver is already a misquote.

**Trap:** "Solely" / "entirely" items collapse a two-factor list into one. Absolute exclusivity words fail whenever the text uses "partly" or an "and" list.

The exclusivity claim contradicts the dual driver in the text, so the statement is false.
highlights: had organised their supply chains around globally dispersed, single-source suppliers operating under justin-time inventory models
exposed a structural vulnerability that had been building quietly for decades
62% reported having reshored or nearshored at least part of their production within the previous three years, a sharp rise from just 24%
seeking geographic proximity without the full cost of domestic production
driven partly by lower transportation costs and reduced exposure to transpacific shipping disruptions

tasks.title: Task 2
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The narrowing US-China labour cost ratio is attributed to a combination of rising Chinese wages and increased automation, not to automation alone.
The labour cost ratio narrowed from roughly 8:1 in 2010 to about 4:1 by 2023, a reduction of half the original gap.
A firm publicly announcing reshoring plans is treated in the passage as functionally equivalent to a firm that has already completed that shift.
The typical delay firms experienced beyond their original reshoring timeline is attributed mainly to falling demand for their products.
The passage treats "friend-shoring" as a more precise label for what is often loosely called "reshoring," rather than as an identical process.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The narrowing US-China labour cost ratio is attributed to a combination of rising Chinese wages and increased automation, not to automation alone.**

Paragraph 4 names both drivers in one phrase: the ratio fell "driven by rising wages in China and by increased automation." Automation is necessary but not sole. The coordinating "and" is the grammatical signal that the claim's "combination…not…alone" reading is correct.

The joint attribution matches the claim, so the statement is true. Do not let a later sentence about labour's shrinking share erase the wage half of the driver list.

**B) The labour cost ratio narrowed from roughly 8:1 in 2010 to about 4:1 by 2023, a reduction of half the original gap.**

The same paragraph gives "roughly 8:1 in 2010" and "about 4:1 by 2023." Halving an 8:1 gap yields 4:1, so the arithmetic paraphrase is faithful. The hedge words "roughly" and "about" still support that simple half-gap reading; they do not invent a different ratio.

The figures and the half-gap reading both fit the passage, so the claim stands. Match both years to both ratios before accepting any numeric paraphrase.

**C) A firm publicly announcing reshoring plans is treated in the passage as functionally equivalent to a firm that has already completed that shift.**

Paragraph 5 separates announcement from completion: of companies that "publicly announced reshoring plans," "only 15% had actually completed the announced shift" on the original timeline. Announcement and completion are precisely not treated as the same. The adverb "actually" in the passage is there to mark the gap the claim erases.

**Trap:** Public intent language often masquerades as done facts in exam items. Treat "announced" and "completed" as different verbs unless the text equates them.

The equivalence claim erases that gap, so it fails.

**D) The typical delay firms experienced beyond their original reshoring timeline is attributed mainly to falling demand for their products.**

Delays are pinned to "permitting delays, skilled-labour shortages, and unexpected construction costs." Falling demand never appears. Those three causes are all supply-side or implementation frictions, not a demand collapse.

The statement invents a demand cause the text does not name, so it is false. If the item swaps in a market-demand story for the named permitting/labour/construction trio, reject it.

**E) The passage treats "friend-shoring" as a more precise label for what is often loosely called "reshoring," rather than as an identical process.**

Paragraph 6 says much of what is "publicly labelled 'reshoring'" "more accurately reflects" moves to allied or trusted third countries, "sometimes termed 'friend-shoring.'" The passage corrects the label; it does not collapse the two into one process. "More accurately" is the precision cue that friend-shoring is the better description of that diversification pattern.

That precision frame matches the claim, so the statement holds. Keep home-country return separate from third-country ally diversification whenever both labels appear.
highlights: driven by rising wages in China and by increased automation
fell from roughly 8:1 in 2010 to about 4:1 by 2023
only 15% had actually completed the announced shift within their originally stated timeframe
often due to permitting delays, skilled-labour shortages, and unexpected construction costs
publicly labelled "reshoring" more accurately reflects diversification toward allied or trusted third countries, a practice sometimes termed "friend-shoring,"

tasks.title: Task 3
tasks.context: Statements test close reading comprehension in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The EU's Chips Act is described as targeting a doubling of the EU's own global semiconductor production share, not an absolute doubling of total global output.
The EU's Chips Act aims to raise the EU's share of global semiconductor production from approximately 20% to 40% by 2030.
Higher domestic labour and compliance costs are cited as the reason reshored production costs more per unit than its offshored equivalent.
The gap between reshored and offshored production costs is described as being absorbed primarily through higher consumer prices.
The continued growth of manufacturing hubs like Vietnam and India is presented as evidence against a simple, one-directional reversal of globalisation.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The EU's Chips Act is described as targeting a doubling of the EU's own global semiconductor production share, not an absolute doubling of total global output.**

Paragraph 7 aims at "doubling the EU's share of global semiconductor production" — a relative slice of the world total, not a doubling of all chips made worldwide. "Share of global…production" is the key noun phrase: the EU wants a bigger percentage of the pie, not a doubled world pie.

Share versus absolute output is the distinction the claim gets right, so it matches the text. Whenever "doubling" appears, check what noun is being doubled — share or total volume.

**B) The EU's Chips Act aims to raise the EU's share of global semiconductor production from approximately 20% to 40% by 2030.**

The passage doubles "from approximately 10% to 20% by 2030." The statement doubles the wrong baseline (20%→40%). Starting from the target instead of the baseline is the exact paraphrase error.

**Trap:** Same "doubling" story, swapped percentages. A correct doubling must keep both endpoints: 10% and 20%, not a shifted pair.

The wrong start and end percentages overturn the claim.

**C) Higher domestic labour and compliance costs are cited as the reason reshored production costs more per unit than its offshored equivalent.**

Paragraph 8 estimates reshored units cost 20–25% more, "reflecting higher domestic labour and compliance costs." That is exactly the reason named. The participle "reflecting" attaches those two cost types directly to the percentage premium.

The cost drivers line up with the statement, so it is true. Do not substitute consumer prices or automation for the named labour-and-compliance explanation of the premium itself.

**D) The gap between reshored and offshored production costs is described as being absorbed primarily through higher consumer prices.**

Only "roughly 3% to 5%" of the gap is passed to consumers; "the remainder" is absorbed via thinner margins or automation gains — so consumers are explicitly not the main sponge. "Modest fraction" already blocks any "primarily" reading that puts retail prices first.

The "primarily through higher consumer prices" reading reverses the text, so the claim fails. Match "primarily" only to whatever the passage treats as the larger share of absorption.

**E) The continued growth of manufacturing hubs like Vietnam and India is presented as evidence against a simple, one-directional reversal of globalisation.**

Paragraph 9 says those hubs' rise suggests networks "may be being rerouted and diversified rather than straightforwardly reversed." Growth elsewhere is offered as a counter to a clean reverse-globalisation story. "Rather than straightforwardly reversed" is the passage's own rejection of a one-way unwind.

That use of the hubs matches the claim, so the statement stands. Treat Vietnam/India growth as diversification evidence, not as proof that nothing moved.
highlights: doubling the EU's share of global semiconductor production from approximately 10% to 20% by 2030
from approximately 10% to 20% by 2030
reflecting higher domestic labour and compliance costs
only a modest fraction of this gap, roughly 3% to 5%, is ultimately passed on to consumers
may be being rerouted and diversified rather than straightforwardly reversed

tasks.title: Task 4
tasks.context: Statements test whether a plausible-sounding inference is actually supported by the passage, ordered by the paragraph each relies on, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: Since automation is named as one factor narrowing the labour cost ratio, it can be concluded that automation alone fully explains the shift.
The labour cost ratio's narrowing from 8:1 to 4:1 is, by simple arithmetic, a reduction of exactly half the original gap.
A firm reporting it has "reshored part of its production" is not automatically the same, by the passage's own logic, as a firm that has completed a full transition.
Because nearshoring benefited Mexico, the passage implies Mexican labour costs converged with those in the United States.
Since reshored production costs more per unit, the passage implies that reduced profit margins are the only way firms can absorb that extra cost.
tactical_explanations:
**A) Since automation is named as one factor narrowing the labour cost ratio, it can be concluded that automation alone fully explains the shift.**

Paragraph 4 lists automation beside rising Chinese wages. Naming "one factor" never licences wiping out the other. The inference upgrades a joint "driven by…and…" list into a sole cause without any passage warrant.

**Trap:** "Since X is mentioned…" leaps to "X is the whole cause." Presence of a factor is not exclusivity of that factor.

The sole-cause leap overreaches the joint drivers, so the inference fails.

**B) The labour cost ratio's narrowing from 8:1 to 4:1 is, by simple arithmetic, a reduction of exactly half the original gap.**

The stated path from "roughly 8:1" to "about 4:1" is arithmetically a halving of the original gap; the claim stays inside that inference. No extra economic story is smuggled in — only the ratio arithmetic the numbers already imply.

The arithmetic follows the passage figures, so the statement is true. Accept half-gap paraphrases when both endpoints match the text; reject them when the endpoints are swapped or rounded into a different story.

**C) A firm reporting it has "reshored part of its production" is not automatically the same, by the passage's own logic, as a firm that has completed a full transition.**

Survey language of reshoring "at least part" of production (Paragraph 2) and the sharp drop from announced plans to completed shifts (Paragraph 5) both warn against equating partial or announced moves with a finished full transition. "At least part" already builds a partial-versus-full distinction into the reporting metric itself.

The caution matches the claim, so it holds. Keep partial reports and full completed transitions as separate statuses whenever the passage uses both framings.

**D) Because nearshoring benefited Mexico, the passage implies Mexican labour costs converged with those in the United States.**

Mexico's benefit is tied to proximity and cost savings versus full US domestic production — not to Mexican wages meeting US wages. Wage-ratio language elsewhere concerns US–China, not Mexico–US. The "because…implies" leap invents a wage-convergence claim the Mexico paragraph never makes.

The wage-convergence implication is unsupported, so the statement fails. Do not transplant Paragraph 4's US–China ratio onto Mexico's nearshoring appeal.

**E) Since reshored production costs more per unit, the passage implies that reduced profit margins are the only way firms can absorb that extra cost.**

Paragraph 8 lists remaining absorption via "reduced profit margins or offset by automation-driven productivity gains" — two paths, not one exclusive door. "Or" after margins is the grammatical block on any "only way" reading.

**Trap:** "Only way" collapses an or-list. Extra cost does not automatically mean a single absorption mechanism.

The exclusivity twist contradicts the dual offset, so the inference is false.
highlights: driven by rising wages in China and by increased automation
fell from roughly 8:1 in 2010 to about 4:1 by 2023
only 15% had actually completed the announced shift within their originally stated timeframe
seeking geographic proximity without the full cost of domestic production
absorbed through reduced profit margins or offset by automation-driven productivity gains

tasks.title: Task 5
tasks.context: Statements require linking details across the passage in paragraph order, with one numeric statement woven in at its correct position.
statements: The gap between high reported reshoring intentions and low actual completion rates suggests some firms discuss reshoring more readily than they execute it.
The average delay of roughly 18 months beyond original targets is consistent with the passage's broader caution against taking announced reshoring intentions at face value.

Because friend-shoring is distinguished from genuine reshoring, and because Vietnam's import share grew, it follows that Vietnam itself has become a genuine reshoring destination for US manufacturers.
The narrowing labour cost ratio helps explain why reshoring has become more feasible, even though the passage still treats reshored production as costlier overall.
Because the passage raises genuine uncertainty about whether this shift is durable, it can be concluded that the statistical trends presented earlier must therefore be considered unreliable.
tactical_explanations:
**A) The gap between high reported reshoring intentions and low actual completion rates suggests some firms discuss reshoring more readily than they execute it.**

Paragraph 5 cautions against taking announced intentions "at face value" and shows only 15% finishing on the stated timeline. That gap between talk and finished relocation supports reading announcements as easier than execution. The face-value warning is the passage's own licence for this talk-versus-done inference.

The synthesis stays inside the passage's own caution, so the claim is true. Do not stretch it into a claim that no firm ever completes a move — only that announcement outruns timely completion.

**B) The average delay of roughly 18 months beyond original targets is consistent with the passage's broader caution against taking announced reshoring intentions at face value.**

The same paragraph pairs the face-value warning with "average delays of roughly 18 months beyond their initial targets." The delay is concrete evidence for that caution, not a rival story. Firms missing the original timeframe by about a year and a half is exactly why announced plans should not be read as finished facts.

The numeric detail reinforces the warning, so the statement holds. Link the 18-month figure back to the caution sentence rather than treating it as a free-standing trivia fact.

**C) Because friend-shoring is distinguished from genuine reshoring, and because Vietnam's import share grew, it follows that Vietnam itself has become a genuine reshoring destination for US manufacturers.**

Vietnam's rising share illustrates "a rerouting… away from China rather than a repatriation of manufacturing to the United States itself." Friend-shoring is third-country diversification; calling Vietnam "genuine reshoring" flips that distinction. The premises are true; the "it follows" conclusion renames diversification as home-country return.

**Trap:** Rising third-country hubs ≠ home-country return. Growth of Vietnam's import share is evidence of rerouting, not of US reshoring.

The conclusion mislabels Vietnam as reshoring, so it fails.

**D) The narrowing labour cost ratio helps explain why reshoring has become more feasible, even though the passage still treats reshored production as costlier overall.**

Paragraph 4 presents the narrowed ratio as making the shift "more feasible," while Paragraph 8 still prices reshored units 20–25% above the offshored equivalent. Feasible-er and still costlier can both be true. Narrower differentials reduce the penalty; they do not erase the remaining premium the later paragraph names.

The two claims coexist in the text, so the synthesis stands. Accept "more feasible yet still costlier" when each half is anchored in its paragraph.

**E) Because the passage raises genuine uncertainty about whether this shift is durable, it can be concluded that the statistical trends presented earlier must therefore be considered unreliable.**

Paragraph 9 debates durability — structural reversal versus temporary shock — without questioning whether the earlier survey percentages or FDI figures are accurate. Uncertain future is not the same as unreliable past data. The "active debate" is about interpretation of the reordering's lastingness, not about whether 62% or $35 billion were miscounted.

The leap from debate-about-future to "statistics are unreliable" invents a charge the text never makes, so the claim fails.
highlights: critics caution against taking announced reshoring intentions at face value
average delays of roughly 18 months beyond their initial targets
rather than a repatriation of manufacturing to the United States itself
cost between 20% and 25% more per unit than the offshored equivalent
remains a matter of active debate among economists

tasks.title: Task 6
tasks.exam_title: Grammar Rules (New Sentences, Anchored in Text Vocabulary)
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "Had firms not diversified their supplier base earlier, the disruption would have proven even more severe."
"The board recommended that the company reassesses its exposure to single-source suppliers."
"The number of manufacturers reconsidering their sourcing strategy continue to grow."
"Neither the subsidy nor the tax credits were enough to fully offset the higher labour costs."
"Having relocated part of its production, the firm reduced its exposure to shipping disruptions."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "Had firms not diversified their supplier base earlier, the disruption would have proven even more severe."**

This is a well-formed third conditional with inverted protasis: "Had firms not diversified…" stands for "If firms had not diversified…," and the main clause correctly uses "would have proven." No auxiliary is missing, and the time sequence (earlier diversification → past disruption counterfactual) is coherent. Inversion after omitted "if" is standard in formal written English for this pattern.

The inverted conditional is formed correctly, so the sentence is sound. Check that past perfect sits in the inverted clause and "would have" + past participle sits in the result clause.

**B) "The board recommended that the company reassesses its exposure to single-source suppliers."**

After "recommended that," English prefers the subjunctive (or mandative) base form: "reassess," not indicative "reassesses." The plural-looking third-person -s marks the wrong mood. The board's recommendation is a demand-like clause, so present-indicative agreement is the wrong reflex.

**Trap:** Normal present-tense agreement after recommend/suggest + that. The subject "company" still takes the bare verb in the mandative pattern.

Repair to "…that the company reassess…," so the line as written fails.

**C) "The number of manufacturers reconsidering their sourcing strategy continue to grow."**

The grammatical subject is singular "The number," so the verb must be "continues," not plural "continue." What follows "of" does not control agreement. "Manufacturers" is only the prepositional complement; it cannot license a plural verb.

Subject–verb agreement collapses here; the sound version is "…continues to grow," so the sentence fails. Train the eye on "the number of" → singular versus "a number of" → plural.

**D) "Neither the subsidy nor the tax credits were enough to fully offset the higher labour costs."**

With "neither…nor," the verb commonly agrees with the nearer noun. Here "tax credits" is plural, so "were" is the expected choice. Had the nearer noun been singular "subsidy," "was" would be the matching form instead.

Proximity agreement is applied correctly, so the wording stands. Always check which noun sits immediately before the verb in a neither–nor pair.

**E) "Having relocated part of its production, the firm reduced its exposure to shipping disruptions."**

The participial opener "Having relocated…" attaches to "the firm," which is logically the relocator — no dangling modifier. Perfect participle plus past main clause is a clean sequence. The -ing phrase names an earlier completed action by the same subject that then "reduced" exposure.

The participle and subject line up, so the sentence is true. Reject the pattern only when the opener's implied agent differs from the main-clause subject.

tasks.title: Task 7
tasks.context: Each sentence is newly constructed, using vocabulary echoing the passage. Decide if each sentence is grammatically correct.
statements: "No sooner had the factory reopened than orders began to resume."
"The subsidy, along with several tax incentives, were introduced to accelerate the transition."
"Each of the surveyed manufacturers have reported some disruption to their supply chain."
"By the time the program concludes, several new facilities will have already opened."
"The data, which were gathered across multiple sectors, point to a broadly consistent pattern."
tactical_explanations:
**A) "No sooner had the factory reopened than orders began to resume."**

"No sooner…than" correctly triggers inversion ("had the factory reopened") and pairs past perfect with a following simple past ("began"). The correlative "than" (not "when") is the right partner. Fronted "No sooner" forces the auxiliary before the subject, which this sentence does.

The correlative inversion pattern is intact, so the sentence holds. Memorise the pair as "no sooner…than," never "no sooner…when."

**B) "The subsidy, along with several tax incentives, were introduced to accelerate the transition."**

"Along with several tax incentives" is a parenthetical add-on; the head subject remains singular "The subsidy," which needs "was introduced," not "were." Commas around the along-with phrase mark it as non-head material that cannot flip agreement.

**Trap:** The nearest plural noun after the comma steals agreement. Ignore "tax incentives" for verb number; stay with "subsidy."

Repair to "…was introduced…," so the written verb fails.

**C) "Each of the surveyed manufacturers have reported some disruption to their supply chain."**

"Each of" takes a singular verb even when a plural noun follows: "has reported," not "have reported." "Each" is the true subject head; "manufacturers" only completes the of-phrase.

Agreement is wrong for "each"; the sentence does not stand. Same singular rule applies to "every" and "either of" in this exam bank.

**D) "By the time the program concludes, several new facilities will have already opened."**

"By the time" plus a future reference point calls for future perfect to mark completion before that point: "will have…opened" is the right shape, with "already" naturally sitting inside it. Simple future "will open" would not mark the before-deadline completion as clearly.

The future-perfect framing fits the deadline, so the wording is true. Use will have + past participle whenever completion is framed as finished by a future milestone.

**E) "The data, which were gathered across multiple sectors, point to a broadly consistent pattern."**

Here "data" is treated as plural throughout: "were gathered" and plural "point" agree with that choice. The relative clause and main verb stay consistent. Switching to singular "was…points" would also be a coherent house style, but mixing plural and singular would not.
